issues.subcategory: Inconsistent Cohen's d conversion from R-squared
issues.description: The manuscript reports ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25 for the SESOI, but earlier in the same paragraph reports the same effect as Cohen's d = .22. These two values are inconsistent: ΔR2 = .012 corresponds to f2 = .012/(1-.012) ≈ .0121, and converting f2 to d via d = 2*sqrt(f2) gives approximately d = .22, not .25. The manuscript uses d = .24 in one place and d = .25 in another for what appears to be the same effect, suggesting arithmetic errors in the effect size conversions that undermine the precision of the SESOI justification.
issues.quote: Prior studies of moral incongruence have found moral incongruence to have small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent f2 values relative to reported ΔR2
issues.description: The manuscript reports ΔR2 = .012 alongside f2 = .016 for the same effect. Cohen's f2 for incremental variance is calculated as ΔR2/(1 - R2_full). For f2 to equal .016 when ΔR2 = .012, the full model R2 would need to be approximately .25. This is plausible but not stated. More critically, ΔR2 = .014 is paired with f2 = .020, which requires a full model R2 of approximately .30. These implicit assumptions about full model R2 are never disclosed, making the effect size conversions unverifiable and potentially misleading. Similarly, ΔR2 = .072 paired with f2 = .12 requires full model R2 ≈ .40, and ΔR2 = .12 paired with f2 = .23 requires full model R2 ≈ .48. None of these full-model R2 values are reported.
issues.quote: Prior studies of moral incongruence have found moral incongruence to have small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020), to moderate (ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen's d = .69; Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020), to relatively large (ΔR2 = .12, f2 = .23, Cohen's d = .97, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020) effects

issues.subcategory: Incorrect Cohen's d derivation from f2
issues.description: The manuscript converts f2 to Cohen's d using what appears to be the formula d = 2*sqrt(f2). For f2 = .12, this gives d ≈ .69, and for f2 = .23, d ≈ .96. While these match the reported values approximately, Cohen's d is not a standard or appropriate conversion from regression f2 in this context—f2 is a regression effect size and d is a mean-difference effect size. They are not directly interchangeable without additional assumptions about the design. Reporting d values derived from f2 in a regression context is methodologically inappropriate and potentially misleading to readers who may interpret these as standardized mean differences.
issues.quote: to moderate (ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen's d = .69; Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020), to relatively large (ΔR2 = .12, f2 = .23, Cohen's d = .97, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020) effects in predicting self-reported problematic pornography use

issues.subcategory: PGSI response scale inconsistency between methods text and supplemental materials
issues.description: In the methods section, the PGSI is described as a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always), and responses are said to be averaged. However, in the supplemental materials, the actual PGSI response options shown are: Never (0), Sometimes (2), Most of the time (4), Almost Always (5). This is not a standard 0-3 scale—the values jump non-linearly (0, 2, 4, 5), which is inconsistent with the original validated PGSI scoring (0, 1, 2, 3) and with the description in the methods text. This discrepancy means the scoring described in the methods cannot be applied to the actual items as presented, creating a fundamental measurement inconsistency.
issues.quote: problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index (Ferris & Wynne, 2001). This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions... on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: BPS scoring inconsistency between methods text and supplemental materials
issues.description: In the methods section, the Brief Pornography Screen (BPS) is described as having a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often), with responses summed. However, in the supplemental materials, the actual response options are Never (0), Occasionally (2), Very Often (4)—a scale with values 0, 2, and 4, not 0, 1, and 2. This means the maximum possible sum score would be 20 (not 10 as implied by the 0-2 description), and the scale is not the standard BPS scoring. This discrepancy between the described and actual scoring undermines the validity of the measure as described and makes replication impossible.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt, 'In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?' by reporting the frequency they have experienced certain behaviors... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: Gambling frequency scale inconsistency
issues.description: In the methods section, gambling frequency is described as assessed on a 6-point scale ranging from 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). However, in the supplemental materials, the actual gambling frequency item uses a scale of Never (0) to More than Once Per Day (5)—a 6-point scale anchored at 0, not 1. This is inconsistent with the methods description and also inconsistent with the pornography frequency scale described as 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). These anchoring discrepancies will affect centering, interpretation of zero-points, and comparability across behaviors.
issues.quote: Participants will be asked how often they have engaged in the behavior over the past 12 months using the same 6-point scale described above, ranging from 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.subcategory: Pornography frequency scale anchor inconsistency
issues.description: The methods section describes pornography viewing frequency as assessed on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). However, the supplemental materials show the actual pornography frequency item anchored at Never (0) to More than Once Per Day (5). This 0-5 scale differs from the 1-6 scale described in the text. This inconsistency affects how the variable will be centered, how non-users are identified (scores > 1 vs. scores > 0), and the interpretation of the interaction term.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). Like the above-described process for the ASSIST, only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months (i.e., scores > 1 on the frequency measure) will complete the remaining items described below.

issues.subcategory: NIDA-ASSIST composite scoring with non-equivalent item scales
issues.description: The NIDA-ASSIST composite score is described as the average of five items: three frequency items scored 0-5 and two yes/no/recent items scored 0, 3, or 6. The manuscript states 'Responses to each of the above five items will be standardized, and an average will be taken.' However, the text also says these will be standardized before averaging, which would address the scale incompatibility. But the standardization approach is only mentioned for the ASSIST composite, not consistently described across all measures. More critically, standardizing within the sample before computing composites means the composite's psychometric properties will be sample-dependent and cannot be compared to validated ASSIST scoring norms.
issues.quote: Participants will also respond to two questions... for each substance on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be standardized, and an average will be taken for each substance of interest

issues.subcategory: Underpowered subgroups acknowledged but analytic plan inadequate
issues.description: The power analysis explicitly acknowledges that prescription drug misuse (estimated n=140) has only 30.1% power to detect the primary SESOI (f2=.015), and illicit substance use (n=240-480) has only 47.2%-76.4% power. The proposed solution—shifting to a larger equivalence region based on the pornography CI lower bound—changes the research question fundamentally for these subgroups. This means the study cannot answer its primary question (is moral incongruence null for these substances?) for two of its seven substance/behavior categories. This is a critical limitation that is underplayed.
issues.quote: However, in the case of illicit drug use (prevalence estimated at 6%-12% of the population) and prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population), it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small

issues.subcategory: Biased oversample distorting gambling analyses
issues.description: The study includes a 1,500-person oversample of sports-wagering individuals added to the 2,500-person nationally representative sample. For gambling analyses, the effective N is listed as 3,325 (73% of 4,000+), but this figure conflates the representative sample with a highly selected clinical/behavioral oversample. Gambling prevalence, frequency, moral disapproval, and problem gambling severity will be systematically different in the sports-wagering oversample compared to the general population. Combining these samples without appropriate weighting or stratification will produce biased estimates of the moral incongruence effect for gambling that cannot be generalized to the U.S. population.
issues.quote: Furthermore, due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: No plan for handling the combined sample in gambling analyses
issues.description: The analytic plan does not specify how the nationally representative sample and the sports-wagering oversample will be handled in the gambling analyses. Will they be analyzed separately? Combined with weights? Combined without adjustment? The power analysis treats them as a single combined sample (effective N = 3,325), but this approach would produce estimates that are not representative of any defined population. The absence of a clear analytic strategy for this fundamental design feature is a major methodological gap.
issues.quote: Gambling | 73% (national sample) 100% (sports-betting oversample) | 3,325

issues.subcategory: Pornography measure restricted to solo use only
issues.description: The pornography frequency measure in the supplemental materials asks only about viewing pornography 'alone (i.e., without a partner).' This operationalization excludes partnered pornography use, which is a common behavior. The methods section and introduction discuss pornography use broadly, but the actual measure captures only a subset of pornography use behavior. This restriction may systematically underestimate pornography use frequency and may introduce selection bias, as those who only use pornography with partners would be classified as non-users and excluded from analyses.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.subcategory: Gambling frequency operationalized as average across behaviors rather than overall frequency
issues.description: The methods state 'To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.' However, the supplemental materials show only a single gambling frequency item ('Gambled or placed bets at all'). There is no multi-item gambling frequency scale to average across. This is either an error in the methods description or the supplemental materials are incomplete. If only a single item is used, the averaging procedure described is inapplicable.
issues.quote: To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: Missing control for non-medical prescription drug use vs. legitimate use
issues.description: The study includes 'prescription drug misuse' as a category, but the frequency item in the supplemental materials asks about 'Prescription Drugs for Non-Medical Reasons' while the moral disapproval item asks about 'using prescription drugs for non-medical reasons.' However, there is no screening or control for whether participants who report prescription drug use are using them medically (legitimately) versus non-medically. Participants who use prescription drugs medically may respond to the frequency item differently than intended, contaminating the non-medical use measure.
issues.quote: Prescription Drug Use/Misuse | Average of modified NIDA-ASSIST items for specific substances

issues.subcategory: No validation of NIDA-ASSIST extension to pornography and gambling
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly acknowledges that including pornography and gambling in the NIDA-ASSIST 'is not currently validated for gambling or pornography.' Despite this acknowledgment, the study proceeds to use these unvalidated items as primary outcome measures for two of its eight key analyses. The justification that 'including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses' is asserted without evidence. The face validity of applying substance use disorder screening items to pornography and gambling is questionable, particularly for items referencing 'use' of a substance.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: Covariates obtained from panel data not survey, creating temporal mismatch
issues.description: Age, gender, and religiousness are described as being obtained from YouGov panel data rather than from the study survey itself. This means these covariates may have been measured at a different time point than the study measures, potentially months or years earlier. For a variable like religiousness, which can change over time, this temporal mismatch could introduce measurement error in a key covariate. Furthermore, the panel religiousness measure may differ from the three-item Pew measure described in the methods, creating a discrepancy between what is described and what will actually be used.
issues.quote: Age, gender, and religiousness will be assessed using panel data provided by YouGov (i.e., not as a part of our survey).

issues.subcategory: No blinding or demand characteristic controls for moral disapproval items
issues.description: Moral disapproval items are presented alongside frequency and addiction measures in the same survey. Participants who have already reported high frequency use and addiction symptoms may respond to moral disapproval items differently than those who have not yet completed those items. The order of item presentation is not specified, and no counterbalancing or separation of morality items from behavioral items is described. This creates potential demand characteristics and order effects that could artificially inflate or deflate the moral incongruence interaction.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography. For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong'

issues.subcategory: Moral incongruence operationalized as statistical interaction, not as perceived discrepancy
issues.description: The manuscript defines moral incongruence as 'the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior.' However, moral incongruence as a psychological construct refers to the subjective experience of discrepancy between one's values and behaviors. A statistical interaction between two variables is not equivalent to a measured psychological construct. High frequency users who strongly disapprove may not subjectively experience incongruence if they have rationalized their behavior. The operationalization conflates a statistical artifact with a psychological experience, which is a fundamental construct validity problem.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with frequency of engaging in the action.

issues.subcategory: Single-item moral disapproval measures lack construct validity evidence
issues.description: All moral disapproval measures are single items ('I believe that [behavior] is morally wrong'). Single items cannot be assessed for internal consistency, and their test-retest reliability and construct validity are unknown in this context. Moral disapproval is a multidimensional construct that may include beliefs about harm, purity, fairness, and religious transgression. A single item asking only about moral wrongness captures only one dimension and may systematically miss important variance, particularly for substances where moral disapproval may be more nuanced (e.g., disapproving of heavy use but not moderate use).
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong' on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: Self-reported addiction conflated with diagnostic criteria
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, 'self-reported feelings of addiction' and 'self-perceived addiction' are used interchangeably with 'addiction,' 'disorder symptoms,' and 'problematic use.' The study measures self-perception, not clinical diagnosis. The BPS and PGSI are screening tools, not diagnostic instruments. The manuscript's framing—particularly its implications for CSBD diagnostic criteria—requires distinguishing between self-perceived problems and clinically validated disorder. The conflation of these constructs undermines the clinical implications drawn throughout.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral incongruence regarding pornography use will predict self-reported feelings of addiction... We expect to find that moral incongruence as it relates to gambling behaviors, will not predict self-reported levels of gambling disorder symptoms.

issues.subcategory: Religiousness measure may not adequately capture moral conservatism
issues.description: The study uses a three-item religiousness measure (importance of religion, prayer frequency, service attendance) as a proxy for moral conservatism in covariates. However, religiousness and moral conservatism are related but distinct constructs. A highly religious person may not morally disapprove of pornography (e.g., progressive religious individuals), and a non-religious person may hold conservative sexual values. Using religiousness as a covariate when the primary predictor is moral disapproval creates potential multicollinearity and conceptual redundancy without adequately separating the constructs.
issues.quote: In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates, as prior work has demonstrated clear links between such variables and self-reported problematic pornography use

issues.subcategory: Causal language used for cross-sectional correlational design
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly uses causal language ('moral incongruence predicts,' 'moral disapproval amplifies,' 'moral incongruence is a clear contributor') for what is explicitly acknowledged to be a cross-sectional design. The limitations section notes 'This sample is cross-sectional, precluding causal inference,' yet the hypotheses, introduction, and discussion sections are framed in causal terms. This inconsistency is particularly problematic given that the study's implications for CSBD diagnostic criteria require causal claims about whether moral incongruence causes false-positive self-reports.
issues.quote: moral disapproval of pornography likely amplifies the links between pornography use and self-reported feelings of compulsivity or addiction... This sample is cross-sectional, precluding causal inference.

issues.subcategory: Reverse causality not addressed for moral disapproval and addiction symptoms
issues.description: The model assumes moral disapproval precedes and causes self-reported addiction feelings. However, it is equally plausible that experiencing addiction symptoms leads individuals to morally disapprove of their own behavior (i.e., reverse causality). Someone who has tried and failed to stop using pornography may subsequently develop moral disapproval as a post-hoc justification or as a consequence of distress. The cross-sectional design cannot distinguish these causal directions, yet the manuscript consistently frames moral disapproval as the antecedent.
issues.quote: moral incongruence is a clear contributor to self-reported feelings of addiction to, compulsivity in, or problems with pornography use. More simply, moral incongruence predicts feeling out of control in one's pornography use.

issues.subcategory: Unaddressed confound: distress as common cause
issues.description: General psychological distress is a plausible common cause of both moral disapproval (distressed individuals may be more morally rigid) and self-reported addiction feelings (distressed individuals report more problems). The manuscript does not include any measure of general psychological distress as a covariate, despite acknowledging that 'self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography is associated with greater psychological distress.' Without controlling for distress, the moral incongruence interaction may be spurious.
issues.quote: Cross-sectionally, self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography is associated with greater psychological distress (Bőthe et al., 2020; Grubbs et al., 2015, 2021)

issues.subcategory: Unaddressed confound: shame and stigma as alternative explanations
issues.description: The manuscript cites literature showing that individuals with gambling disorder 'view their behaviors to be a moral failure' and that substance users experience stigma and self-stigma. These phenomena (shame, stigma, self-stigma) are alternative explanations for the relationship between moral disapproval and self-reported addiction that are distinct from moral incongruence. The study does not include measures of shame or stigma, and the analytic plan does not address how to distinguish moral incongruence effects from shame/stigma effects.
issues.quote: there is certainly evidence that many individuals with substance use disorders morally disapprove of their own behaviors (Matthews et al., 2017) and that individuals with gambling disorder often view their behaviors to be a moral failure (E. Miller & Thomas, 2017; Hing et al., 2016).

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis numbering system is inconsistent and confusing
issues.description: The hypotheses are presented as a numbered list but use an inconsistent numbering scheme. The text refers to 'hypotheses 2b and 3b' in the analytic plan, but the hypotheses as written are not formally numbered with such a scheme in the text. The hypotheses appear to be: H1 (pornography moral incongruence predicts addiction), H1a (direct effect of disapproval), H1b (interaction effect), H2 (gambling moral incongruence does not predict), H2a (direct effect significant), H2b (interaction not significant), H3 (substance moral incongruence does not predict), H3a (direct effect significant), H3b (interaction not significant). This numbering is implied but never stated, making the analytic plan difficult to follow.
issues.quote: Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction for moral disapproval of a behavior and frequency of that behavior fall fully within our equivalence region, we may reasonably conclude that the true effect is so low as to be null or practically null, thereby supporting hypotheses 2b and 3b, listed above.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction between stated goal and hypothesis structure
issues.description: The stated purpose is 'to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior.' However, Hypothesis 2a predicts that the direct effect of moral disapproval of gambling WILL significantly predict gambling problems, and Hypothesis 3a predicts the same for substances. If moral disapproval directly predicts addiction symptoms for gambling and substances (H2a, H3a), this already demonstrates that moral disapproval is not unique to sexual behavior—contradicting the stated goal. The authors cannot simultaneously claim uniqueness while predicting significant direct effects for other behaviors.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral disapproval of gambling among gamblers will positively predict self-reported gambling problems, even when including gambling frequency, religiousness, gender, and age as covariates in a regression model... Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior

issues.subcategory: Total number of analyses inconsistent across sections
issues.description: The methods section states 'we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validated measures.' However, Table 1 lists 7 target behaviors/substances (alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, pornography, gambling). With pornography and gambling each analyzed twice, this gives 5 + 2 + 2 = 9 analyses, not 10. The discrepancy between 8 'target behaviors/variables' and 7 listed in Table 1, and between 10 stated analyses and 9 derivable from the design, is unexplained.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validate measures of problematic use

issues.subcategory: SESOI reference value inconsistency between sections
issues.description: In the SESOI justification section, the reference effect for the equivalence region is described as coming from Grubbs, Lee, et al. (2020) with β=.11. However, later in the same section, when describing the fallback equivalence region for underpowered analyses, the reference shifts to Grubbs, Kraus, et al. (2020) Study 1 Sample 3 with β=.270. The manuscript then states the lower bound of the 95% CI for this effect is .23. But earlier it states 'β = .27, 95% CI [.23, .31], ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12.' This creates confusion about which effect and which study serves as the primary benchmark.
issues.quote: we will test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate of moral incongruence in predicting self-reported addiction to pornography (β = .27, 95% CI [.23, .31], ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen's d = .69; Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020)

issues.subcategory: Survey item order not specified
issues.description: The order in which survey items will be presented to participants is not specified anywhere in the manuscript or supplemental materials. Given that the study measures moral disapproval, behavioral frequency, and addiction symptoms for the same behaviors, item order could substantially affect responses through anchoring, demand characteristics, and consistency motives. This is a critical omission for a registered report, as the order should be pre-specified to prevent post-hoc adjustment.
issues.quote: Key measures described below are available in supplemental materials submitted with this Stage 1 Registered Report proposal.

issues.subcategory: No specification of how multiple testing will be controlled across 10 analyses
issues.description: The study plans to conduct 10 moderation analyses. The manuscript mentions 'Holm-adjusted test statistics' for bivariate correlations but does not specify any multiple testing correction for the primary moderation analyses. With 10 tests at α=.05, the familywise error rate is approximately 40%. The absence of a pre-specified multiple testing correction strategy for the primary hypotheses is a significant reporting gap that could lead to inflated Type I error rates.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

issues.subcategory: No specification of how to handle participants who use multiple substances
issues.description: Many participants will use multiple substances (e.g., alcohol and cannabis). The analyses treat each substance independently, but the manuscript does not address how comorbid use will be handled. Participants who use multiple substances may have systematically different moral disapproval profiles, and the independence assumption of separate regression models may be violated. No plan for addressing this dependency is described.
issues.quote: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be restricted to those who have engaged in the behavior within the past year. That is, we will only administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to participants who report engaging in those behaviors.

issues.subcategory: Criteria for 'substantial' assumption violations not pre-specified
issues.description: The analytic plan states that 'in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses.' However, 'substantially violated' is not operationally defined. No thresholds, tests, or criteria are provided for determining when a violation is substantial enough to trigger the supplemental latent variable analyses. This leaves a researcher degree of freedom that could be exploited post-hoc.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: No pre-specification of how to handle non-binary gender in analyses
issues.description: The analytic plan specifies that gender will be coded as binary (1 = male, 0 = not-male) for analyses. However, the YouGov panel data likely includes non-binary gender options, and the study is described as nationally representative. The manuscript does not address how non-binary participants will be classified, whether they will be excluded, or how this binary coding decision affects the representativeness of the sample. This is particularly relevant given the study's focus on sexual behavior.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: No description of how the sports-wagering oversample was recruited or defined
issues.description: The manuscript states that 1,500 adults with 'recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically' will be recruited. However, no details are provided about how this oversample will be identified, recruited, or screened. Will they be YouGov panel members who self-report sports wagering? Will there be a screening question? What counts as 'wagering on sports'? The absence of these details makes the composition of this critical subsample unclear.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically.

issues.subcategory: Missing details on how SPSS standardization will be performed before R analyses
issues.description: The analytic plan describes a two-software workflow where SPSS is used for data transformation and standardization, and R is used for analyses. However, the specific standardization procedures (z-scoring within the full sample vs. within behavior-specific subsamples, handling of missing data during standardization) are not described. Given that analyses will be conducted on subsamples of users, standardizing in the full sample versus the user subsample will produce different results.
issues.quote: Data will be provided by YouGov in SPSS format. Accordingly, SPSS will be used to transform the above-described ASSIST items and measures of religiousness into standardized variables.

issues.subcategory: Sports-wagering oversample undermines representativeness claims
issues.description: The manuscript claims to use 'a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500)' but the total analytical sample includes 1,500 non-representative sports-wagering individuals. For gambling analyses specifically, the combined sample (n=3,325) is dominated by the oversample and cannot be considered representative. Yet the manuscript's conclusions about gambling moral incongruence will be drawn from this combined, non-representative sample. The public significance statement and conclusions do not acknowledge this limitation.
issues.quote: This work will make use of an upcoming study (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500).

issues.subcategory: U.S.-only sample limits generalizability to other cultural contexts
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that 'moral incongruence as it relates to pornography use does appear to vary somewhat by the cultural context in which it is studied.' However, the study is conducted exclusively in the U.S., and the conclusions are framed as broadly applicable to CSBD diagnostic criteria (ICD-11), which is an international classification system. The U.S. has a particularly high rate of religious conservatism compared to other Western nations, which may inflate moral incongruence effects for pornography relative to other countries.
issues.quote: Although a nationally representative sample in the U.S. is better than convenience sampling methods, such a sample represents only one broad cultural context in which these hypotheses could be tested.

issues.subcategory: Findings from community sample inappropriately extrapolated to clinical settings
issues.description: The manuscript's primary motivation is to inform CSBD diagnostic criteria and clinical practice. However, the study uses a community/population sample. The manuscript acknowledges that 'the effects of moral incongruence on feelings of addiction are most critical in treatment seeking populations' but proceeds to draw clinical implications from community data. The relationship between moral incongruence and self-reported addiction may be substantially different in treatment-seeking populations, where true dysregulation is more prevalent.
issues.quote: despite the ability of the present study to evaluate whether or not moral incongruence affects self-reported feelings of addiction a population level, it is likely that the effects of moral incongruence on feelings of addiction are most critical in treatment seeking populations.

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis predicts null effects for gambling/substances but also predicts significant direct effects—theoretical inconsistency
issues.description: The theoretical framework predicts that moral incongruence (the interaction) is unique to pornography, but simultaneously predicts that the direct effect of moral disapproval will be significant for gambling and substances. This creates a theoretical inconsistency: if moral disapproval directly predicts addiction symptoms for gambling and substances, then morality IS relevant to these addictions, which undermines the claim that the ICD-11 caveat about moral distress is unique to CSBD. The theoretical model needs to explain why the direct effect of moral disapproval is expected to generalize but the interaction is not.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral disapproval of gambling among gamblers will positively predict self-reported gambling problems... However, we do not expect to find that the interaction of moral disapproval of gambling and gambling frequency will significantly predict self-reported gambling disorder symptoms.

issues.subcategory: Misapplication of PPMI model to substances with different addiction mechanisms
issues.description: The PPMI model was developed specifically for pornography use, where the addictive potential is debated and moral/religious factors are particularly salient. Applying this model to substances like nicotine and alcohol, which have well-established neurobiological addiction mechanisms, requires theoretical justification that is not provided. The neurobiological compulsion to use nicotine is qualitatively different from the psychological experience of pornography use, and the role of moral disapproval in these contexts may be fundamentally different for reasons beyond mere statistical interaction.
issues.quote: we seek to establish whether moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior) influences self-perceived feelings of addiction to both behaviors (i.e., gambling) and substances (alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, and illicit drugs).

issues.subcategory: Conflation of moral incongruence with moral disapproval throughout
issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently uses 'moral incongruence' and 'moral disapproval' as if they are interchangeable. Moral incongruence is defined as the interaction of disapproval and frequency, but throughout the introduction and discussion, statements about 'moral disapproval predicting addiction' are described as evidence for 'moral incongruence.' For example, the meta-analytic finding that 'moral disapproval of pornography among pornography users was the most substantive predictor' is cited as support for the PPMI model, even though this is a direct effect, not an interaction.
issues.quote: Using such a conceptualization, meta-analytic findings demonstrated that moral disapproval of pornography among pornography users was the most substantive predictor of self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography (Grubbs, Perry, et al., 2019).

issues.subcategory: Claim that CSBD is the only diagnosis with a moral distress caveat may be inaccurate
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly asserts that 'CSBD is the only recognized disorder in any diagnostic manual to include such a caveat' about moral distress. However, this claim is not substantiated with a systematic review of all diagnostic criteria across ICD-11 and DSM-5. Several other diagnoses (e.g., paraphilic disorders, some religious/spiritual problems) have related considerations. The claim is presented as established fact but is actually an empirical assertion that requires verification.
issues.quote: CSBD is the only recognized disorder in any diagnostic manual to include such a caveat, pointing to the unique role of morality in shaping feelings of compulsivity in or addiction to sexual behaviors.

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc equivalence region redefinition creates researcher degrees of freedom
issues.description: The analytic plan includes a pre-specified fallback procedure: 'In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.' This means the equivalence region will be determined by the pornography result obtained in the same study, creating a circular and data-dependent equivalence test. The pornography CI lower bound is unknown before data collection, so this procedure cannot be fully pre-specified.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: Undisclosed decision rules for choosing between OLS and latent variable models
issues.description: The analytic plan states that if regression assumptions are 'substantially violated,' latent variable models will be used instead. However, the decision of which results to present in the main text ('we will present OLS results and corresponding graphs in text, with supplemental analyses included as appendices') is contingent on results 'remaining robust.' The definition of 'robust' (same sign and significance) is specified, but this still allows for a scenario where the researcher chooses between two analytic approaches based on whether they agree, which is a form of analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results and corresponding graphs in text, with supplemental analyses included as appendices/supplemental materials.

issues.subcategory: No pre-specification of what happens if OLS and latent variable results diverge
issues.description: The analytic plan specifies what to do if results are robust across methods (present OLS in text), but does not specify what to do if results diverge between OLS and latent variable models. If the interaction is significant in OLS but not in the latent variable model (or vice versa), there is no pre-specified decision rule for which result to report as primary. This is a critical gap in the registered analytic plan.

issues.subcategory: Unrealistic assumption of zero missing data
issues.description: The manuscript states 'we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data' based on YouGov's quality control procedures. This is an unrealistic assumption for any survey study. Even with high-quality panel data, item-level missingness occurs due to skip logic errors, participant fatigue, sensitive item refusal, and technical issues. The absence of any missing data plan (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation, full information maximum likelihood) is a significant methodological gap that could affect results if missingness is not random.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: No plan for handling participants who skip moral disapproval items
issues.description: Moral disapproval items ask participants to rate whether behaviors are 'morally wrong.' Some participants may refuse to answer these items (particularly for sensitive behaviors like illicit drug use or pornography) or may select 'neither agree nor disagree' as a non-response. The manuscript does not address how missing or neutral responses to moral disapproval items will be handled, nor does it consider whether the midpoint of the moral disapproval scale (4 = neither agree nor disagree) represents genuine neutrality or item avoidance.

issues.subcategory: Differential exclusion across behaviors creates non-comparable subsamples
issues.description: The study restricts each analysis to past-year users of each behavior. This means each analysis uses a different subsample with potentially different demographic and psychological characteristics. For example, the alcohol subsample (70% of sample) will be much larger and more demographically diverse than the illicit drug subsample (6-12%). The manuscript acknowledges 'slightly different subsets' but does not address how the non-comparability of these subsamples affects the interpretation of cross-behavior comparisons, which is the central goal of the study.
